# Project summary and structure

The goal of this project is to make declaration data easy to search, browse and interpret.

- `exposed/` contains the rust application and CLI code that powers the project.
- `frontend/` contains a simple Svelte application
- `ingest/` contains the legacy Python scripts used to bootstrap this project.

## Exposed coding policy

- Follow with strict detail to the existing style of the application. This includes:
  - Type driven design
  - Domain modelling and parse-not-validate
  - Consistent error handling
  - Service layer abstractions

- Interactions with the database must use `sqlx` macros for compile-time query verification.

- For Rust changes, read and apply the
  [Rust domain development skill](.agents/skills/rust-domain-development/SKILL.md).
- Before implementation, identify the domain states, invariants, and the type
  that owns each rule. Parse external values into those types at boundaries and
  retain typed values internally.
- Use one canonical domain enum for each finite vocabulary. Do not duplicate
  its variants in string allowlists. Use exhaustive matches where behavior
  depends on a variant.
- When a bug exposes duplicated domain rules, remove the duplication rather
  than synchronizing the copies. Trace changes through producers, serialization,
  consumers, and persistence together.

## Frontend coding policy

- The frontend is largely in a prototype stage so changes can be made freely without much guidance.
- Every PR that changes the UI must include desktop screenshots in its
  description. Capture the affected views from the running application on
  the PR branch after completing the changes.
- Upload screenshots as GitHub attachments with `gh pr create --attach` or
  `gh pr edit --attach`. Use a GitHub CLI version that supports this flag. Never
  commit PR screenshots to the repository. Verify that the attachments render
  in the PR description before marking the PR ready for review.


## Ingest coding policy

- When porting code from this project, do not replicate the style. Use it as an end to end guide for functionality.

## Worktree policy

- For read-only tasks (investigating, reading, summarizing, or describing code),
  work on the current branch without creating a worktree.
- For tasks that require changing code or other files, work in a dedicated Git
  worktree before making changes. If a read-only task expands to require changes,
  switch to a dedicated worktree first.
- For such changes, reuse this chat's dedicated worktree if one already exists.
  Otherwise, create a sibling worktree with a unique branch and perform all
  edits, installs, and checks there.
- Never modify the primary checkout.
- Report the worktree path and branch when starting work in a dedicated worktree.

## Git history

- After completing and validating a task, commit its changes on the task's work
  branch without waiting for a separate request.
- Never commit directly on `main`.
- Keep Git history linear. Rebase feature branches onto the target branch and
  integrate changes with a fast-forward or squash; do not create merge commits.

## Development database migrations

- Keep schema changes in `db/migrations` as SQLx versioned `.up.sql` and
  `.down.sql` pairs. From the repository root, create a pair with
  `sqlx migrate add --source db/migrations --reversible <name>`.
- Never change a migration file that existed before the current PR. Treat those
  migrations as immutable, even when they have not been applied locally.
- When a PR's schema design changes, you must edit, consolidate, or remove the
  migrations introduced by that PR. Do not append a corrective migration for an
  obsolete step in the same PR. Before review, the PR must contain only the
  migrations needed for its final schema. Recreate isolated test databases that
  applied a discarded PR migration; do not preserve obsolete steps just to
  satisfy their checksums.
- Do not fold changes into the baseline or put manual schema scripts in
  `db/upgrades`.
- From the repository root, apply migrations with
  `sqlx migrate run --config sqlx.toml --source db/migrations`, inspect them with
  `sqlx migrate info --config sqlx.toml --source db/migrations`, and revert the
  latest version with
  `sqlx migrate revert --config sqlx.toml --source db/migrations`.
  Commands read the root `.env`; set `DATABASE_URL` to select another database.
- SQLx owns each migration transaction. Do not add `BEGIN` or `COMMIT` to the
  migration files. Keep each down migration limited to its up migration's changes.
- Test forward upgrades with existing records and the full down/up cycle in an
  isolated database. Preserve imported data when upgrading an existing database.
- The one-time transition from the consolidated baseline requires schema and
  data verification before aligning its checksum. Follow `db/README.md`;
  changing the checksum alone does not apply schema changes.

</INSTRUCTIONS>

# Daily declaration synchronization

This is a proposed architecture. No application code or schema has changed.

The recommendation is incremental acquisition with complete-snapshot interpretation. Discover changed members, reacquire their complete declaration histories, merge retained raw evidence, then run global cleaning, resolution, and atomic loading. Keep the first implementation compatible with existing resolution semantics. Fully incremental resolution is a separate investment.

## Options

| Approach | Acquisition | Interpretation and publication | Main tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Full acquisition with content diff | Every stored member | Rebuild when evidence changes | Smallest departure, no remote acquisition saving |
| Changed-member acquisition with complete snapshot | Full histories of affected members | Complete corpus | Recommended first version. Reuses member partitions and retains global context |
| Changed-interest acquisition with complete snapshot | Unfiltered records for discovered IDs | Complete corpus | Less acquisition, more relationship, ownership, and record-merge handling |
| Fully incremental processing | Changed records | Affected dependencies and identity components | Requires durable evidence, identity merge/split rules, reverse dependencies, and global alias maintenance |

No runtime or cost reduction has been measured. Complete resolution and grouping remain global work.

## Proposed caller experience

```sh
exposed data declarations sync --config CONFIG
exposed data declarations sync --config CONFIG --reconcile
exposed data declarations sync --config CONFIG --resume RUN_ID
```

Daily sync bootstraps a complete capture if there is no committed base. Reconciliation scans the retained member cohort again. Resume continues a sealed run without changing its evidence under the same run ID. Existing stage commands remain replay and inspection tools. They cannot bypass generation validation when publishing to the synchronized projection.

## Acquisition and snapshot

Read the committed generation and discovery checkpoint from Postgres. Freeze an inclusive date window with configurable overlap and indexing lag. The source exposes dates, so the boundary must define its calendar policy explicitly. Query publication and update windows separately, then union their results. Registration dates are not correction timestamps.

Filtered responses identify changed members. Fetch their complete histories without date filters, with expired records included and children separate. Add newly stored members even when discovery is empty. Unknown discovered members must be loaded and fully backfilled, or fail the run visibly; never silently skip them. Preserve former members already in the retained scope.

Observed API behavior makes hydration necessary. For interest 14513, an update-filtered list returned register 822 only. The same list endpoint filtered solely by InterestIds returned registers 822 and 794. The filtered response therefore cannot replace complete raw evidence. Probe responses are retained beside this document. This observation does not prove the behavior of every API query.

Merge reacquired records into immutable member partitions keyed by DeclarationId, checking member ownership. Retain old records missing from a response as discrepancies until withdrawal semantics are established. Snapshot manifests reference all member partitions, including reused immutable files. Record hashes, query policy, cohort, capture times, discovery receipts, and expected base generation. Materialize the complete snapshot for current stage readers. Do not relabel old evidence as freshly fetched. Compare canonical content separately from retrieval timestamps.

Only seal a capture after every planned member and page completes. Stage files under unique names and publish after closing and verifying them. Reject HTTP errors, inconsistent pagination, duplicate conflicting records, and truncated responses. Use bounded retries. Offset pagination has no documented transactional snapshot guarantee; overlap and periodic reconciliation reduce this risk but do not prove losslessness.

## Interpretation and publication

Run existing global clean and resolve over the complete merged snapshot. This retains parent evidence, reconsiders children whose parents changed, and derives company aliases from all surviving observations. Publish the complete resolved projection, because changed identity components can affect declarations outside the source delta.

Prepare durable immutable artifacts before the database transaction. Inside the existing declaration-loader lock, check the expected base generation, load the projection, rebuild groups, record the snapshot reference and fingerprints, and advance the discovery checkpoint in one transaction. An already committed run returns its recorded result before checking its old base. A stale base rejects publication and requires rebuilding against the current generation.

A crash before commit leaves the old checkpoint and projection. Resume can reuse sealed artifacts. A crash after commit returns the committed result. A successful empty scan advances coverage without replacing evidence or changing funder identities. Every checkpoint commit increments a publication revision, including empty scans. Expected-base checks use this revision so a concurrent empty scan cannot move coverage backwards. Artifact retention pins every partition referenced by the committed snapshot. Production storage must survive scheduler replacement; the database projection cannot reconstruct complete source evidence.

## Domain ownership and sketch

```rust
enum SyncMode { Daily, Reconcile }
struct DiscoveryWindow { /* checked inclusive source dates */ }
struct PublishedGeneration { /* generation, snapshot reference, coverage */ }
struct CompleteCapture { /* privately constructed from verified traversal */ }
struct PreparedPublication { /* expected base, run, snapshot, load fingerprint */ }
enum PublishOutcome { Committed(SyncReport), AlreadyCommitted(SyncReport), StaleBase }

impl DeclarationSyncService {
	async fn synchronize(&self, mode: SyncMode) -> Result<SyncReport, EntityIngestionError>;
	async fn resume(&self, run: IngestionKey) -> Result<SyncReport, EntityIngestionError>;
}
```

These are signatures for discussion, not implemented Rust. Reuse DeclarationId, MemberId, IngestionKey, and existing errors. The domain model owns scope and completeness rules. The sync service owns orchestration. The Parliament adapter owns queries and external parsing. The artifact adapter owns immutable snapshot files. The existing load repository owns the atomic publication transaction and SQLx queries. Add versioned reversible migrations for checkpoint, generation, and run publication metadata when implementation is approved.

Model the Domain changes the design to explicit complete-capture and prepared-publication states. Make Operations Idempotent changes the publication protocol to atomic checkpoint advancement, exact-run replay, and expected-base checks.

## Limits and acceptance

Current noncompany identity strings contain the ingestion key. A complete re-resolution can therefore change funder IDs and URLs, as full refreshes already can. This proposal preserves matching semantics, not stable external identity IDs. Stable IDs require explicit cross-generation identity reconciliation and merge/split policy.

Neither a delta omission nor an empty member response authorizes deletion. Periodic full reconciliation reports omissions and catches updates missed by discovery. A future explicit retirement policy must remove projection records transactionally. Validate update coverage, indexing delay, and pagination behavior before treating the discovery checkpoint as a completeness guarantee.

Acceptance checks should compare baseline plus delta with a fresh full capture under the same evidence and policy. Compare semantic outputs rather than generation-specific IDs. Include parent-only updates, historical aliases, funding reorder, unknown/new members, empty scans, interrupted capture, load rollback, exact retry, and competing publication. Fully incremental resolution remains an option when measured processing costs justify it.

# Architect

On Codex, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/codex-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill.

On GitHub Copilot, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/copilot-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill.

Design before implementing. Sketch types, function signatures, class shapes, and module boundaries with `not implemented` bodies and pseudocode. Synthesize across multiple model perspectives, then fill in code against the chosen sketch. If implementation proves the sketch wrong, throw it out and redesign.

## Start

Open a todolist with one entry per phase before starting.

1. Ground
2. Sketch
3. Agree
4. Implement
5. Scrap

## Phase A: Ground the problem

Build a real mental model of every system the new code touches. Run the **how** skill over the relevant subsystems.

Naming a file isn't grounding. Produce the traced model `how` prescribes. If the design redefines ownership or layering, also run the **why** skill on the existing shape so the rationale becomes a constraint, not a guess.

Skip Phase A only when the work is genuinely greenfield with no surrounding system to integrate.

You are one of several runners, each on a different model. Produce the best design your model can make. Don't hedge against the others. Differences between candidates are the signal used to pick a base and graft. Converging on a safe-looking middle defeats the exploration.
# Design red flags

Screen every candidate before synthesis. A red flag is a reason to revise or reject the shape.

## Shallow module

A shallow module exposes a large interface while hiding little complexity. Judge depth by the capability and policy hidden behind the public surface relative to the size of that surface. Prefer a simple interface backed by substantial behavior.

Do not confuse a deep module with a deep call chain. A deep call chain scatters understanding across layers. A deep module concentrates capability behind one interface.

Look for these signs:

- Callers coordinate several methods to complete one operation.
- Public options expose internal stages or implementation choices.
- Learning the interface does not save the caller from learning the implementation.

## Information leakage

Information leakage makes multiple modules depend on the same internal decision. A representation, policy, or protocol detail appears in more than one place, so changing it requires coordinated edits.

Public re-exports of transport or wire types are leakage. Parse external data into domain types behind the interface. Keep storage schemas, framework objects, and protocol details private.

## Temporal decomposition

Temporal decomposition organizes modules by execution order instead of the knowledge they own. Separate load, validate, transform, and save stages often repeat one representation and its invariants across several boundaries.

Group code around domain knowledge and ownership. Methods that run at different times can still belong to one module when they protect the same decisions.

## Pass-through method

A pass-through method forwards the same arguments to another method with the same shape. It adds a layer without hiding complexity.

Remove it or move responsibility to the module that can complete the operation. Keep a forwarding boundary only when it adds policy, adaptation, or a distinct abstraction.

## Split ownership

More than one module writes the same state or keeps its own copy of it. An agent that edits one writer can't see the others, so their rules diverge.

Give each piece of state one owner. Other modules read it or ask the owner to change it.

## Two ways to do one task

The design supports more than one way to do the same task. An agent copies whichever way it finds first, so every way keeps gaining callers.

Keep one way. Move callers off the others and delete them in the same change.

## Importable internals

A caller can import a module's internals. An agent takes the shortest path that compiles, so it imports them directly and they become part of the interface.

Make internals unreachable from outside the module, so an import from outside fails the build.

## Hand-synced list

Two or more places list the same items, and adding an item means editing every list. An agent that sees one list updates only that one.

Keep one list and derive the others from it. If a list can't be derived, make the build fail when the lists disagree.
